data.text/html:
Logarithms: turning multiplication into addition

Based on Eigen: "This Is the Logarithm Explanation You Never Got". One idea runs through the whole lesson: write down how many times a number was multiplied by itself, and add those counts instead of multiplying the numbers.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eColour language used throughout\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cspan style=\"color:#2e86ab\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eblue = numbers\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e: the top row, the world where we \u003cem\u003emultiply\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cspan style=\"color:#f18f01\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eorange = counting numbers / exponents / logarithms\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e: the bottom row, the world where we \u003cem\u003eadd\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cspan style=\"color:#e4572e\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ered = the answer\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e you are hunting for\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
1. The doubling trick

400 years ago, multiplying two big numbers by hand could take most of a day. The question was: can multiplication be turned into addition? Start with powers of two: ||(2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, \dots||) Each number is the last one times two. Under each one, write how many twos were multiplied to build it, the counting number: ||[\underbrace{2\cdot2\cdot2}_{3\text{ twos}} \cdot \underbrace{2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2}_{4\text{ twos}} = \underbrace{2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2}_{3+4=7\text{ twos}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 8\times16 = 128||]Multiplying on top is the same as adding on the bottom. Click any two numbers on the top row below.

The trick does not care about the base.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
2. The problem with the gaps

The top row ||(2, 4, 8, 16, 32||) is spread far apart. What if we want ||(7 \times 12||)? Neither is on the row; they fall in the gaps. So we loosen what "counting number" means. ||(7||) sits between ||(8 = 2^3||) and ||(4 = 2^2||), close to ||(8||), so its counting number should be a bit under ||(3||). The video says "something like 2.8", and indeed ||(2^{2.8} \approx 6.96||). Predict first: what counting number sits under 7?
Make your guess, then lock it in.

A half-count of twos is a square root.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3. Turning it into a curve, then flipping it

Plot exponent → number and you get the exponential curve ||(y = 2^x||): slow at first, then faster and faster. But we want the opposite: hand it a number (say 7) and get its exponent back. So we swap the axes. Every point ||((x, 2^x)||) becomes ||((2^x, x)||), a mirror image across the diagonal ||(y = x||). That flipped curve is Napier's table drawn with no gaps. Its name is the logarithm: ||[\log_2(N) = \text{the exponent you raise 2 to in order to reach } N, \qquad \log_2 32 = 5.||]Drag the blue point along the exponential curve; its orange mirror rides along the logarithm.

Same pair, coordinates swapped.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eLook at the orange curve's shape: from 2→4→8 the number doubles each time while the log only goes up by \u003cstrong\u003e1\u003c/strong\u003e. Huge numbers get squeezed into small heights.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag to x = 0: every base gives 1, so \u003cstrong\u003elog(1) = 0\u003c/strong\u003e for any base. Drag below 0: numbers between 0 and 1 have \u003cem\u003enegative\u003c/em\u003e logs.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4. Multiply by just adding

The rule that is "the entire reason the logarithm exists": ||[\log(A\cdot B) = \log A + \log B||]and the ones that fall out for free: ||[\log\frac{A}{B} = \log A - \log B, \qquad \log(A^n) = n\,\log A \;\;(\text{so } \sqrt[3]{A} \text{ becomes } \tfrac{1}{3}\log A).||]Napier's readers did it like this: look up two logs, add, then look up backwards which number has that sum. Walk through it step by step:

step what you do result
1. look up log2(32) and log2(8) 5.0000 and 3.0000
2. add 5.0000 + 3.0000 = 8.0000 8.0000
3. look up backwards 28.0000 256
check direct calculation 256 ✅

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe video's example: \u003cstrong\u003e32 × 8\u003c/strong\u003e in base 2 → 5 + 3 = 8 → 2⁸ = 256. \"We never once multiplied.\"\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eChange the base to \u003cstrong\u003e10\u003c/strong\u003e or \u003cstrong\u003ee\u003c/strong\u003e: the logs change, the final answer doesn't. The base is just the ruler's units.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eCube root: pick \u003cstrong\u003eA = 1000\u003c/strong\u003e, \u003cstrong\u003eB = 1/3 ≈ 0.3333\u003c/strong\u003e, power. Multiplying the log by ⅓ is \"a cube root as a plain division\".\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5. The slide rule: adding lengths multiplies numbers

Take a ruler, but space the marks by their logarithm: 1, 2, 4, 8 sit equally far apart, because each is one step up in exponent. Put two such rulers next to each other and slide one along the other. To multiply ||(3 \times 4||): put the 1 of the top ruler over 3 on the bottom ruler, then read the bottom ruler under 4 on the top ruler. The lengths add, ||(\log 3 + \log 4 = \log 12||), so the reading is 12. For ~300 years, bridges, ships' tables and early rockets were worked out this way. Drag the top ruler left/right, and drag the red hairline to read off products.

Equal ratios = equal distances.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6. Where logarithms show up today

Some things grow by multiplying: populations, money earning interest, sound energy, earthquake shaking. On a normal axis the curve "shoots off the top of the page". Plot the logarithm instead, and runaway growth straightens into a line, with even, readable steps.

Sound: why "twice as loud" is about ten times the energy

Decibels are a log scale: ||(\text{dB} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{E}{E_0}\right)||). Every +10 dB = ×10 energy, and our ears hear roughly +10 dB as "twice as loud". Earthquake magnitudes work the same way.

From 60 to 120: energy ×1,000,000.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
7. Sandbox: be Napier for a minute

Type any list of positive numbers and pick a base. The notebook multiplies them only by adding logs, like a 17th-century calculator, and plots the log curves of several bases. Notice they are all the same shape, just rescaled: ||(\log_b x = \dfrac{\log_{10} x}{\log_{10} b}||). That is why the base is a choice of units, not a different idea.

The sum of logs stays small while the product blows up.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet the base to exactly \u003cstrong\u003e10\u003c/strong\u003e and multiply 1000, 100: logs 3 + 2 = 5. That's Briggs' \"round, clean steps\".\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eFind a base where log of 2 is 1 and log of 8 is 3. (Then try e ≈ 2.7, the \"natural\" base the video leaves hanging.)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>
